country.comment: Study examines piped water access in Ouagadougou, the capital city of Burkina Faso, drawing on a nationally representative survey of Burkina Faso.

effect_estimate.comment: Hazard ratios and p-value thresholds (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, d p < 0.15) are reported; 95% confidence intervals and standard errors are not reported in the paper.
effect_estimate.value: In Cox proportional hazards models of first piped water (PW) access (N = 2,134 at risk, 232 events) and first PW loss (N = 1,226 at risk, 294 events in Table 1; p. 12 states N = 1,220), housing tenure and urban zoning strongly interact. Without zone interactions, tenants have higher hazard of gaining PW than owners/co-owners (HR = 2.56, p < 0.001, Model 1a) and lower hazard of losing PW (HR = 0.53, p < 0.001, Model 2a). Accounting for zone and tenure-by-zone interactions (Models 1b and 2b), water network connection is impossible in non-zoned areas: among owners, living in the non-zoned periphery vs zoned periphery sharply reduces PW gain (HR = 0.14, p < 0.001) and increases PW loss (HR = 15.38, p < 0.001), whereas living downtown increases PW gain (HR = 3.12, p < 0.001) and lowers PW loss (HR = 0.26, p < 0.001). Renters have higher PW gain than owners only in the zoned periphery (HR = 2.94, p < 0.01; downtown HR = 0.88, ns; non-zoned periphery HR = 0.00, p < 0.001) and face higher PW loss than owners in the non-zoned periphery (HR = 6.31, p < 0.01; zoned periphery HR = 1.43, p < 0.15; downtown HR = 1.67, p < 0.15). Across N = 2,839 Ouagadougou respondents, 80% never changed PW status; 75% of first gains occurred via residential move and 25% via new in-dwelling connection, while 97% of first losses occurred via moving (often to acquire unzoned peripheral property) and 3% via in-dwelling loss, mostly disconnection for water bill non-payment.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational longitudinal event-history design (design ceiling <= 2 under CODEBOOK §9). Rated 1 (documented statistical and descriptive association) because the survey establishes strong statistical associations between residential tenure, urban zoning status, and transitions into/out of piped water (plus descriptive reporting of in-dwelling disconnections for non-payment), but does not directly observe the legal or administrative connection, zoning, or disconnection processes empirically.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–15, Explanatory Variables and Results

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines housing tenure (owner vs tenant), property acquisition in unallocated peripheral areas from traditional chiefs prior to formal zoning allotment, zoning rules prohibiting water network connection in non-zoned areas, urban planning and spatial service-area disparities (ONEA shared water management prioritizing public standpipes/boreholes), high connection fees and monthly charges, and disconnection due to non-payment of water bills.

publication_year.comment: Published in Urban Studies 50(6): 1292–1310, May 2013 (copyright 2012 Urban Studies Journal Limited; paper first received August 2010, in final form July 2012).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational longitudinal time-to-event (retrospective cohort / event-history) study without an intervention comparator: outcome-free risk sets at age 15 or city arrival are tracked across person-time with time-varying exposures until incident transition or right-censoring and analyzed with Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards regression. Life-history trajectories were collected retrospectively in the 2000 EMIUB survey using an age–event calendar.
risk_of_bias_tool.value: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

sample_size.comment: Unit of analysis is the individual across residential life-course spells. Descriptive residential sequence probabilities in Figure 1 use the 2,839 respondents interviewed in Ouagadougou. Note a minor discrepancy in the text between Table 1 (1,226 persons at risk for first loss) and p. 12 prose (1,220 people: 901 with piped water in their first Ouagadougou unit and 319 who gained access later).
sample_size.value: 3,133 individuals with residential episodes in Ouagadougou (2,839 interviewed in Ouagadougou and 294 interviewed outside Ouagadougou) from a national survey of ~9,000 individuals aged 15–64; Cox subsamples: 2,134 individuals at risk for first access (232 events; 255,057 person-time units) and 1,226 individuals at risk for first loss in Table 1 (294 events; 103,963 person-time units; p. 12 text states 1,220 individuals)
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, Data; PDF p. 7, Table 1; PDF p. 9, Figure 1; PDF p. 11, Table 2; PDF p. 12, Loss of Piped Water; PDF p. 14, Table 5

study_design.comment: Reconstructs longitudinal residential, marital, and employment trajectories from age 15 (or arrival in Ouagadougou after age 15) from the 2000 EMIUB retrospective survey to model waiting times to first piped water access and first loss of piped water.
study_design.value: Retrospective longitudinal event-history study (two-stage stratified probability life-history survey using an age–event calendar, analyzed with Kaplan–Meier survivor curves and semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards regression models with time-varying covariates)
